Le cardiomyocyte en est couvert : façonn: The cardiomyocyte is covered with them: shaped by caveolin 3, its caveolae concentrate receptors and channels and serve as a membrane reserve when the cell is stretched.
Deux chaînes α et deux chaînes β, soudée: Two α chains and two β chains, joined by disulfide bridges. Without insulin its outer part draws an inverted V, feet apart: the two kinases, in the cytosol, are too far from each other. Insulin tips it into a T: the feet come together, the kinases phosphorylate each other, then phosphorylate the IRS proteins. Through PI3-kinase and Akt, the cardiomyocyte then brings GLUT4 glucose transporters to its surface: after a meal, the heart burns more glucose.
Un récepteur à sept hélices, couplé à la: A seven-helix receptor, coupled to the Gs protein. Noradrenaline, released by sympathetic fibres, lodges between its helices; the receptor activates Gs, whose α subunit goes off to stimulate adenylate cyclase. Cyclic AMP (yellow) activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the calcium channel, phospholamban and troponin I: the heart beats more strongly, and relaxes faster. The activated receptor is then phosphorylated, capped by β-arrestin and internalised by a clathrin-coated pit: this is the way into this cell.
De −85 mV à un battement : un courant ve: From −85 mV to a heartbeat: a current coming from the sinoatrial node opens the sodium channels, the calcium plateau triggers the release of calcium, troponin C unmasks actin, the sarcomeres shorten, then the calcium is put away and the cell repolarises. Through gap junctions, the impulse passes from cell to cell; through the atrioventricular node, the bundle of His and the Purkinje network, it reaches both ventricles almost at the same time. Each step has its hereditary diseases: the “Genetics” cards of each step name their genes.
Dix-huit étapes, du canal ionique au cœu: Eighteen steps, from the ion channel to the whole heart. We start from a patch of membrane of the cell you are in: resting potential, then the four phases of the cardiac action potential, traced on an oscilloscope. We then follow calcium to troponin C and the shortening of the sarcomere, then the impulse from cell to cell through gap junctions. A long zoom out finally leads to the wall of the ventricle and to the whole heart, with its conduction tissue and its electrocardiogram. Everything is drawn at its real size; the shapes of the proteins and of the heart are schematic. Drag to turn around the scene, use the wheel or pinch to zoom.
Voici le cœur vu de face, battant au ral: Here is the heart seen from the front, beating in slow motion, with its electrocardiogram; the yellow glow is the passage of the impulse. At 70 beats per minute, it beats about 100,000 times a day. With each beat, the left ventricle ejects nearly 80 mL of blood, a little more than half of what it contains (ejection fraction close to 60%): about 5 litres per minute at rest. The muscle is fed by the coronary arteries (bright red), which arise from the aorta: the left anterior descending and the circumflex on the left, and the right coronary artery. Even at rest, the left ventricle extracts 70 to 80% of the oxygen they deliver. An adult heart weighs about 330 g in men, 250 g in women. Turn it around.
Toutes les cellules des ventricules sont: All the cells of the ventricles are now on their plateau (orange): the trace returns to zero, this is the ST segment. Calcium is released everywhere, the ventricles contract together and drive the blood into the aorta and the pulmonary trunk. Then the cells repolarise: this is the T wave. Repolarisation does not simply retrace activation: the regions whose action potential is shortest repolarise early, so that the T wave points in the same direction as the QRS. From the start of the QRS to the end of T, the QT interval: about 360 to 460 ms once corrected for heart rate.
Les ventricules · segment ST et onde T: The ventricles · ST segment and T wave
Sorti du nœud, l'influx s'engage dans le: On leaving the node, the impulse enters the bundle of His, which divides along the septum into a right bundle branch and a left bundle branch (the latter into two fascicles, anterior and posterior). They branch out beneath the endocardium into the Purkinje network: cells poor in myofibrils and rich in connexin 40, which conduct several times faster than the muscle. Within a few tens of milliseconds, the whole endocardium is reached. The wave then crosses the wall from the inside outwards; the last regions to be excited are the base of the left ventricle and the outflow tract of the right ventricle. The whole process lasts about 80 ms: this is the QRS complex. Our cell (turquoise dot) has just been excited.
Faisceau de His et réseau de Purkinje: Bundle of His and Purkinje network
L'influx gagne les deux oreillettes de p: The impulse spreads step by step through both atria, at 0.7–1 m/s: this is the P wave of the electrocardiogram. The atria contract and finish filling the ventricles. Between atria and ventricles, a ring of fibrous tissue does not conduct electricity: the only way through is the atrioventricular node (golden, at the base of the septum). Its cells conduct very slowly and hold the impulse back for 80 to 100 ms. This delay — the flat segment between P and QRS — gives the ventricles time to fill. From the P wave to the QRS, the PR interval lasts 120 to 200 ms.
Les oreillettes, puis le nœud auriculo-v: The atria, then the atrioventricular node
D'où vient le courant qui a excité notre: Where does the current that excited our cell come from? From this small cluster of cells (golden), in the wall of the right atrium. The cells of the sinoatrial node have no stable resting potential: after each beat, the “funny” current If (HCN4 channel) and an internal calcium clock slowly depolarise them up to the threshold (the gentle slope, on the oscilloscope). At the centre of the node, the upstroke of the action potential is carried by calcium channels, not sodium channels: it is slow. Left to itself, the node would beat about a hundred times a minute in a young adult (118 − 0.57 × age); at rest, the vagus nerve slows it down, and during exercise the sympathetic system speeds it up.
Oreillette droite, au pied de la veine c: Right atrium, at the foot of the superior vena cava
Le champ s'élargit. Les cellules devienn: The field of view widens. The cells become fibres, and we discover that their direction rotates steadily through the thickness of the wall: from about +60° near the endocardium (on the inside) to −40 or −60° near the epicardium (on the outside), passing through the horizontal around the middle, where our cell lies. Thanks to this helical winding, the ventricle does not merely tighten: it twists, the apex turning some twenty degrees relative to the base, like a cloth being wrung out. Pull back a little further, and this wall about one centimetre thick finds its place: it is that of the left ventricle, in the whole heart (here in glass, to see inside).
Zoom arrière : la paroi, puis le cœur: Zooming out: the wall, then the heart
Des centaines de cellules, toutes aligné: Hundreds of cells, all aligned. The impulse starts from one point and spreads as an ellipse: it runs two to three times faster along the fibres than across them, because gap junctions are concentrated at the ends of the cells. The myocardium thus behaves like one large cell — a functional syncytium: as soon as one point is excited, all the healthy tissue around it will be too. That is why a scar, which does not conduct, or a tissue where junctions become sparse, can deflect the wave, or even make it circle back on itself.
Reculons encore : voici notre cellule et: Let us pull back further: here are our cell and its neighbours, attached end to end by intercalated discs (dark plates). Three junctions sit side by side there: gap junctions for the current, desmosomes and adherens junctions to hold the cells together when they pull. The action potential (yellow) runs along one cell, crosses the disc, reaches the next: at about half a metre per second, it takes roughly a quarter of a millisecond per cell. Behind the front, the cells stay depolarised (orange) throughout the plateau: the impulse cannot turn back.
Notre cellule et ses voisines · scène la: Our cell and its neighbours · scene 500 µm wide
Au bout de la cellule, sa membrane (à ga: At the end of the cell, its membrane (left) faces that of the next cell (right). In a gap junction plaque, the two membranes are only a few nanometres apart, and channels cross both of them: each is made of two hemichannels of six connexin 43 molecules, one per cell, joined end to end. Ions pass directly from one cytoplasm to the other. The cell on the left has just depolarised: positive charges flow towards the one on the right, which reaches its threshold, opens its own Nav1.5 channels and fires in turn. Each channel conducts little (60 to 100 pS), but a plaque brings together a large number of them. Connexin 43 is renewed constantly: its half-life is about an hour and a half in the rat.
Jonctions communicantes : le courant pas: Gap junctions: the current gets through
Pour que le cœur se relâche et se rempli: For the heart to relax and fill, calcium must leave the cytosol. The SERCA2a pump (blue) sends most of it back into the reticulum — about two thirds to three quarters in the rabbit, and roughly as much in humans — using ATP. Its brake, phospholamban (pink), is released when it is phosphorylated under the effect of adrenaline: the heart relaxes faster. The NCX exchanger (mauve) expels almost all the rest from the cell, bringing in three Na⁺ (yellow) for each Ca²⁺. Troponin C releases its calcium, tropomyosin covers actin again: the sarcomere relaxes.
Dyade et réticulum longitudinal · scène: Dyad and longitudinal reticulum · scene 500 nm wide
À cette échelle, on voit le sarcomère en: At this scale, the whole sarcomere is visible. The thin filaments start from the Z-discs; the thick filaments, 1.6 µm long, occupy the centre, linked by the M-line. When the myosin heads pull, no filament shortens: they slide between one another. The Z-discs move closer together, the I band (thin filaments only) shortens, the A band (thick filaments) keeps its length. Titin (grey springs), the largest known protein, links each thick filament to the Z-disc: stretched during filling, it pulls the sarcomere back to its length. The more the sarcomere is stretched at the start, the more it responds to calcium: this is the basis of the Frank–Starling law. For legibility, the filaments are drawn much further apart than in reality.
Un sarcomère, d'une strie Z à l'autre ·: One sarcomere, from one Z-disc to the next · about 2 µm
Le calcium diffuse jusqu'aux myofilament: Calcium diffuses to the myofilaments. On the thin actin filament (pink), the sites where myosin could attach are masked by tropomyosin (pale ribbon), held in place by the troponin complex. One Ca²⁺ binds to troponin C (golden) — the protein made by this cell's gene, TNNC1. In the heart, only one of its sites acts as the trigger. Troponin I (blue) then lets go of actin to hold on to troponin C, and tropomyosin slides aside. The myosin heads of the thick filament (violet) attach, swing by about ten nanometres, each using one ATP, detach and start again: the thin filament is pulled towards the centre of the sarcomere. The first heads to attach help to push tropomyosin further aside.
Filament fin et filament épais · scène l: Thin filament and thick filament · scene 150 nm wide
Reculons d'un cran. Le potentiel d'actio: Let us pull back a notch. The action potential plunges into the cell along the T-tubules, infoldings of the membrane (on the left, it lights up). There, only 12 to 15 nm away, lies a cisterna of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, full of calcium: together they form a dyad. A few Ca²⁺ enter through the Cav1.2 channels of the tubule and bind to the ryanodine receptors RyR2 (green) facing them, in clusters of about fifteen. The RyR2 open and release the calcium of the cisterna: each cluster produces a “calcium spark”. All the dyads of the cell light up together, and free calcium in the cytosol rises from about 0.1 µM to a little under 1 µM.
Tubule T et réticulum sarcoplasmique · s: T-tubule and sarcoplasmic reticulum · scene 500 nm wide
Les canaux calciques se referment et les: The calcium channels close again and the potassium currents prevail: IKr does most of the work in the human ventricle, IKs serves as a reserve, then Kir2.1 (IK1) completes the descent and restores the resting state. The Nav1.5 channels then lose their plug. Until then, for almost the whole duration of the action potential, the cell could not be re-excited: this is the refractory period. It prevents contractions from fusing and gives the heart time to fill.
C'est la signature du cœur. Pendant plus: This is the signature of the heart. For more than two hundred milliseconds, two currents balance each other: Ca²⁺ (orange) enters through the Cav1.2 channels (ICaL current), K⁺ leaves through the hERG (IKr) and KCNQ1 (IKs) channels, which open slowly. The potential therefore stays close to 0 mV. This plateau makes the action potential last about 250 to 400 ms in humans (235 ms measured in vivo), about a hundred times longer than that of a neuron. The calcium that enters will trigger contraction.
À peine le sommet atteint, un courant po: As soon as the peak is reached, a transient potassium current, Ito (Kv4.3 channel and its KChIP2 subunit), lets a little K⁺ out: the potential dips slightly and draws a notch. It is more marked in cells near the epicardium than in those of the endocardium. Meanwhile, the Cav1.2 calcium channels begin to open.
Un courant arrive de la cellule voisine: A current arrives from the neighbouring cell (white charges, beneath the membrane) and depolarises the membrane up to the threshold. The Nav1.5 channels (SCN5A gene) open: Na⁺ (yellow) pours in, and the potential exceeds 0 mV within one to two milliseconds. The charges carried by the two faces of the membrane are reversed. Almost at once, the channels inactivate by themselves (orange plug): they will be able to reopen only once the membrane has repolarised. The oscilloscope is very stretched out here: it shows only five milliseconds.
Vous êtes devant un morceau de la membra: You are in front of a patch of the cell's membrane, seen in cross-section: the outside at the top, the cytoplasm at the bottom. At rest, the inside is negative, close to −85 mV. Two proteins see to this. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (golden) expels three Na⁺ and brings in two K⁺ for each ATP: it maintains the gradients. The Kir2.1 channel (IK1 current), open at rest, lets a little K⁺ (violet) leak out: it is what sets the potential close to the equilibrium potential of potassium. All the other channels are closed. On the oscilloscope, the line is flat.

Transcytose : enfermé dans une cavéole c: Transcytosis: enclosed in a caveola on the blood side, you cross the endothelial cell and come out in the interstitium of the myocardium. Head for the cardiomyocyte ◎.
Endothélium continu, sans fenêtre : aucu: Continuous endothelium, with no fenestrae: no way through here. Reach the golden ring (◎ marker) to cross by transcytosis.
Dans le cardiomyocyte, qui ne se renouve: In the cardiomyocyte, which is hardly ever renewed, mitophagy continuously removes worn-out mitochondria.
Le cardiomyocyte en a besoin pour ses mi: The cardiomyocyte needs it for its mitochondria, but tolerates an excess poorly: iron overload is a cause of cardiomyopathy.
Dans le cardiomyocyte, c'est la desmine: In the cardiomyocyte, it is desmin: it links the Z-discs to one another, to the membrane, to the nucleus and to the desmosomes. Its variants cause cardiomyopathies and myofibrillar myopathies.
Dans le cardiomyocyte, l'essentiel de l': In the cardiomyocyte, most of the actin is elsewhere: in the thin filaments of the sarcomeres.
Un axone du système nerveux sympathique,: An axon of the sympathetic nervous system, studded with varicosities that release noradrenaline close to the cardiomyocytes. It binds to the β1 receptors: the heart beats faster and more strongly. It is through this receptor that the ship enters the cell.
The heart houses its own macrophages. They clear debris and the mitochondria that cardiomyocytes eject. In the atrioventricular node, they slot in between the conducting cells, to which they are coupled by connexin 43; in the mouse, removing them slows conduction.
Des fibres de collagène, surtout de type: Collagen fibres, mostly type I (strong) and type III (more compliant), weave a sheath around each cardiomyocyte (endomysium) and around the bundles (perimysium). They transmit force, prevent overstretching and align the cells. Their excess, fibrosis, stiffens the heart and hinders the passage of the impulse.
Petite cellule aux longs prolongements,: A small cell with long processes, slipped in between the cardiomyocytes. It makes and renews the collagen of the matrix. After an infarction, fibroblasts multiply and fill the destroyed area with a scar: the lost muscle is not replaced.
Les cardiomyocytes sont attachés bout à: Cardiomyocytes are attached end to end by intercalated discs, and they branch: they form a continuous network, in which the current passes from cell to cell through gap junctions. About 140 µm long, they most often have a single nucleus (74%), sometimes two (25%). They are hardly ever renewed: about 1% per year at age 25, 0.45% at 75 — fewer than half are replaced over a lifetime. They occupy most of the volume of the myocardium, but make up only a third to a half of its cells.
Cellule murale enchâssée dans la lame ba: A mural cell embedded in the capillary basal lamina, which it grips with its processes. It stabilises the wall and helps to adjust its diameter.
L'endothélium continu des capillaires du: The continuous endothelium of the heart's capillaries is rich in caveolae. They can detach from one face of the cell and fuse with the other: in mice lacking caveolin 1, the endothelium no longer takes up or transports albumin. This is one of the routes by which albumin and what it carries cross a wall without fenestrae.
Le cœur se nourrit lui-même : les artère: The heart feeds itself: the coronary arteries arise from the aorta, just above the valve, and branch down to these capillaries. The left ventricle is perfused mainly during diastole, when the relaxed muscle no longer squeezes its vessels. The wall can only be crossed by transcytosis (golden ring, ◎ marker). The “Travel by blood” button takes you to another organ.
Lumière d'environ 5 µm : les globules ro: A lumen of about 5 µm: red cells pass through one by one. The endothelium is continuous, with no fenestrae, resting on a basal lamina. The myocardium is one of the tissues richest in capillaries (2,000 to 3,000 per mm² in the human left ventricle): even at rest it extracts 70 to 80% of the oxygen delivered to it, and can hardly extract more when effort increases; it then needs more flow.
Dans le cardiomyocyte, le noyau est étir: In the cardiomyocyte, the nucleus is stretched and compressed with every beat: variants of LMNA, the gene for lamins A and C, are a common cause of dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction disorders.
Pigment d'usure : résidus lysosomaux non: Wear-and-tear pigment: undigestible lysosomal residues (oxidised lipids and proteins). As the cardiomyocyte almost never divides, they build up with age at the poles of the nucleus.
Petite invagination de la membrane, de q: A small invagination of the membrane, a few tens of nanometres across, shaped by caveolin 3 and the cavins (cavin 4 in muscle). It concentrates receptors and channels, and serves as a membrane reserve when the cell is stretched.
Une ceinture de protéines qui arrime cha: A belt of proteins that anchors each Z-disc to the membrane, then to the basal lamina: on one side the dystrophin complex, on the other the integrins with talin and vinculin. It transmits force to the sides of the cell. Without dystrophin (Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies), the membrane tears and a dilated cardiomyopathy sets in.
C'est ici que les myofibrilles s'accroch: This is where the myofibrils attach to the end of the cell: N-cadherin links the two membranes, and the catenins link it to the actin filaments of the last sarcomere. The force of contraction thus passes from one cell to the next.
Un rivet entre deux cellules. Les cadhér: A rivet between two cells. The cadherins desmoglein 2 and desmocollin 2 span the intercellular space; on the cytosolic side, plakoglobin, plakophilin 2 and desmoplakin link them to the desmin filaments. Variants of their genes cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.
Une plaque de canaux qui relient directe: A plaque of channels that directly connect the cytosol of two neighbouring cells. Each channel is made of two hemichannels of six connexin 43 molecules (GJA1 gene). Ions pass through them: the depolarisation of one cell thus reaches the next, and the whole myocardium contracts like a single cell. Connexin 43 is renewed very quickly: its half-life is about 1.3 hours in the adult rat heart.
La jonction entre deux cardiomyocytes mi: The junction between two cardiomyocytes placed end to end, in a staircase pattern. Three kinds of junction sit side by side there: adherens junctions, where the actin filaments of the last myofibrils are anchored; desmosomes, where desmin is anchored; gap junctions, through which the electrical current passes. In mammals, adherens junctions and desmosomes are largely fused into a mixed junction, the area composita. The Nav1.5 sodium channels are also concentrated there.
Une citerne du réticulum sarcoplasmique: A cisterna of the sarcoplasmic reticulum apposed to a T-tubule. On one side of a 12 to 15 nm cleft, the L-type calcium channels (Cav1.2) of the tubule; on the other, clusters of ryanodine receptors (RyR2), about fifteen on average in the rat. The small amount of calcium that enters through the former opens the latter: the reticulum releases its store. This is calcium-induced calcium release.
Une invagination du sarcolemme, large d': An invagination of the sarcolemma, about 250 nm wide (measured in the rat), mostly at the level of the Z-discs, which carries the action potential into the heart of the cell: without it, the myofibrils at the centre would contract late. Its membrane is rich in L-type calcium channels (Cav1.2).
Le disque qui borne le sarcomère. Les fi: The disc that bounds the sarcomere. The thin filaments of two neighbouring sarcomeres are anchored there, in opposite orientations, cross-linked by α-actinin. Titin has its N-terminal end there; desmin links the Z-discs of neighbouring myofibrils to one another and aligns them. The T-tubules plunge into the cell at this level.
Les filaments fins, longs d'environ 1 µm: The thin filaments, about 1 µm long, are made of actin. Tropomyosin runs along their groove and, at rest, masks the sites where myosin could attach. Every seven actin monomers, a complex of three troponins: T attaches it to tropomyosin, I maintains the block, C binds calcium. It is troponin C that this cell's gene makes. Titin, a giant elastic protein (up to 38,138 amino acids, the largest in the body), extends from the Z-disc to the M-line and crosses the I band: it brings the sarcomere back to its resting length.
Chaque filament épais, long d'environ 1,: Each thick filament, about 1.6 µm long, brings together a few hundred myosin molecules, whose heads project towards the thin filaments. In the human ventricle, it is almost exclusively the β heavy chain (MYH7 gene). Once calcium has freed their sites on actin, the heads attach to them, swing while hydrolysing ATP and pull the thin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere. Myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3) restrains and regulates them. MYH7 and MYBPC3 are the two genes most often involved in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Un cylindre d'environ 1 µm de diamètre f: A cylinder about 1 µm in diameter made of sarcomeres placed end to end, from one intercalated disc to the other. Myofibrils occupy about 60% of the cell's volume. Dark bands (A): thick myosin filaments. Light bands (I): thin actin filaments, carrying tropomyosin and the troponins. Discs: Z-discs. Shrink the ship: the card describes the band you are in. The “⚡ Follow the cardiac impulse” button shows the filaments at work.
pH 4,5–5, hydrolases acides. Il recycle: pH 4.5–5, acid hydrolases. It recycles worn-out mitochondria and sarcomere proteins. The cardiomyocyte hardly divides any more: whatever is not digested accumulates.
Tube creux de 25 nm : 13 protofilaments: A hollow 25 nm tube: 13 protofilaments of α/β-tubulin dimers. In the cardiomyocyte, they form a lattice between the myofibrils and serve as tracks to deliver channels and connexins to the membrane and the intercalated discs.
Elles occupent environ un quart du volum: They occupy about a quarter of the cell's volume in humans (a third in the mouse, whose heart beats ten times faster), lined up in rows between the myofibrils, beneath the membrane and at the poles of the nucleus. The heart never stops: every day it uses about 6 kg of ATP, twenty times its own weight. Its mitochondria burn mainly fatty acids, but also glucose, lactate, ketone bodies and amino acids.
Aux deux pôles du noyau. Il achève et tr: At both poles of the nucleus. It finishes and sorts membrane proteins and packages the natriuretic peptides into secretory granules.
Le réticulum lisse du muscle : un mancho: The smooth reticulum of muscle: a sleeve of tubules around each myofibril, ending in cisternae apposed to the T-tubules. It is the calcium store for contraction. The SERCA2a pump brings calcium back into it after each beat, held back by phospholamban as long as the latter is not phosphorylated; calsequestrin retains it there.
Peu développé, surtout près du noyau. Il: Poorly developed, mostly near the nucleus. It makes membrane proteins (channels, pumps, receptors) and the natriuretic peptides, which the heart secretes when its wall is stretched: ANP in the atria, BNP in the ventricles.
Plusieurs ribosomes 80S traduisent le mê: Several 80S ribosomes translate the same mRNA. Free polysomes make the proteins of the sarcomere — myosin, actin, troponins, titin — which are renewed continuously without the cell ceasing to beat.
Autour du noyau, les myofibrilles s'écar: Around the nucleus, the myofibrils part and leave a cone of cytoplasm at each pole: it contains the Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, reticulum, lysosomes and, with age, lipofuscin granules. Everywhere else, the cell is almost entirely filled with myofibrils and mitochondria.
Après son activation, le récepteur β1 es: After its activation, the β1 receptor is phosphorylated by the kinase GRK2; β-arrestin binds to it, cuts off the signal and takes it into a clathrin-coated pit. This is how the cell desensitises when stimulation is prolonged.
Récepteur à sept hélices transmembranair: A receptor with seven transmembrane helices (ADRB1 gene), coupled to the Gs protein. Noradrenaline released by sympathetic fibres, or adrenaline from the blood, makes it activate adenylate cyclase; cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the L-type calcium channel, phospholamban, the ryanodine receptor and troponin I. The heart contracts more strongly and relaxes faster. Beta-blockers occupy this receptor without activating it.
La membrane du cardiomyocyte. Au repos,: The membrane of the cardiomyocyte. At rest, the Kir2.1 potassium channels and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump hold it at around −85 mV. It carries the Nav1.5 sodium channels, which trigger the action potential, and the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger; it plunges into the cell as T-tubules, mostly at the level of the Z-discs. Costameres anchor it to the myofibrils, and small invaginations, the caveolae, concentrate receptors and channels. The “⚡ Follow the cardiac impulse” button shows one beat.
Vous êtes entre les cellules du muscle c: You are between the cells of the heart muscle. Each cardiomyocyte is wrapped in a basal lamina (laminin, collagen IV), then in a fine network of collagen fibres, the endomysium, which links it to its neighbours and to the capillaries. The myocardium is one of the best-perfused tissues: 2,000 to 3,000 capillaries per mm² in the human left ventricle, roughly one per cell. Here you come across fibroblasts, which maintain the matrix, resident macrophages and the fibres of the sympathetic nervous system.
Endosome précoce : le récepteur y est dé: Early endosome: the receptor is dephosphorylated there, then recycled to the surface or sent to the lysosome if stimulation persists. Meanwhile, protein kinase A has phosphorylated the calcium channel, phospholamban and troponin I: the heart beats more strongly and faster.
Le récepteur activé stimule la protéine: The activated receptor stimulates the Gs protein and the production of cyclic AMP, then it is phosphorylated by the kinase GRK2; β-arrestin binds to it and takes it, with AP-2, into a clathrin-coated pit.
Liaison au récepteur β1-adrénergique : l: Binding to the β1-adrenergic receptor: the ship passes itself off as a noradrenaline molecule, the messenger of the sympathetic nervous system.
Vous arrivez par le sang dans un capilla: You arrive with the blood in a capillary of the myocardium, the muscle of the heart. Its wall is continuous, with no fenestrae: reach the golden rings ◎ and cross by transcytosis, then make for the cardiomyocyte, where other rings mark the entrance. The “Take me to the entrance” button takes you there.

Condensat de forme irrégulière (20 à 50: Irregularly shaped condensate (20 to 50 per nucleus) made of 20–25 nm interchromatin granules. At the core (pink): the proteins SON and SRRM2, without which it dissolves. Around them: SR proteins (cyan) and snRNPs (blue). At the periphery: the long non-coding RNA MALAT1 (orange). No DNA and no transcription inside: it is a reserve of splicing factors in constant exchange with the nucleoplasm.

Six exons, 161 codons : la troponine C c: Six exons, 161 codons: cardiac troponin C (the same as that of slow skeletal muscle). Two lobes linked by a helix; each carries two “EF-hand” motifs. In the N lobe, only one site still binds calcium (site II; site I is inactive): it is the sensor that triggers contraction at every beat. Calcium alone does not open this lobe: it allows it to grasp a short segment of troponin I, which then lets go of actin. The two sites of the C lobe, always occupied by Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺, anchor the protein to the thin filament. Rare TNNC1 variants are associated with hypertrophic (p.Ala8Val, p.Leu29Gln, p.Cys84Tyr, p.Asp145Glu) or dilated (p.Gly159Asp) cardiomyopathies.
Très court. Transcrit mais non traduit :: Very short. Transcribed but not translated: the ribosome scans from the cap to the first AUG.
Un enhancer accolé au promoteur, étudié: An enhancer adjoining the promoter, studied in the mouse, drives expression in the heart: it carries several binding sites (CEF-1, CEF-2 and three CPF sites), one of which binds GATA-4; mutating CEF-1 or CEF-2 switches it off. A second enhancer, in the first intron, drives expression in slow skeletal muscle. The loop brings the factors bound to the enhancer close to the promoter.
Non-canonical TATA box (TATTTAA, −30). In the mouse, a short promoter–enhancer (positions −124 to +32) is enough to switch the gene on in heart cells; the transcription factor GATA-4 binds there. More broadly, sarcomere genes depend in the heart on a network of factors that work together: GATA4, MEF2, NKX2-5, TBX5, SRF and its partner myocardin. The same gene is also used in the slow fibres of skeletal muscle.
